Credit: Marjorie Schott, NLR, with components from Pond5.com Regardless of the application, all refrigerants share a common purpose—to move heat from one location to another. In practice, there are a variety of chemicals that do this, and their properties can be dramatically different. ASHRAE Standard 341 defines toxicity and flammability properties for refrigerants (Figure 2). Some refrigerants have been or are being phased out of use or are not yet commonly adopted across equipment types. In addition, some refrigerants work better at certain temperatures than others. 1https://www.ashrae.org/file%20library/technical%20resources/standards%20and%20guidelines/standards%20adde nda/34_2019_f_20191213.pdf 1 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies (NLR) at www.nlr.gov/publications. Safety classification. Because refrigerants are used in buildings, their relative toxicity and flammability are important safety indicators. These parameters have standard classifications described in Figure 2. Figure 2. Toxicity and flammability classifications of refrigerants as defined by ASHRAE Standard 34 Credit: Marjorie Schott, NLR Toxicity is described using alphabetical designations. Class A indicates refrigerants with low toxicity and class B indicates refrigerants with high toxicity. Flammability is classified according to flame spread speeds, and ASHRAE Standard 34 uses this information to characterize flammability. One (1) indicates no flame propagation, 2L indicates low flammability, 2 indicates flammability, and 3 indicates high flammability. Common refrigerants. There are many common refrigerants, and Table 1 describes a sampling of them as well as their classifications and types, ozone depletion potential (ODP), global warming potential (GWP), and current status or use. Natural refrigerants are a class of refrigerants that are not hydrofluorocarbons (HFCs), can exist naturally, and are not derived as a manufactured product. GWP values reference the atmospheric heating impact relative to carbon dioxide (CO ), which 2 has a GWP value of one. In other words, one pound of R-22 has the same impact as 1810 pounds (approximately one ton) of CO . Newer refrigerants have GWP values closer to one or zero. 2 Because of the wide variety of refrigerant applications and classifications, it is important to develop a refrigerant management plan to track locations, types, and quantities of refrigerants throughout a facility or a portfolio of facilities. 2 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies (NLR) at www.nlr.gov/publications. ODP values reference the amount of degradation a chemical can cause to the ozone layer relative to trichlorofluoromethane (CFC-11, also referred to as R-11). R-11 has an ODP of 1.0.2 Newer refrigerants have ODP values of zero or close to zero. Note that the scale of measurement is different between GWP and ODP. Table 1.
